title: An effective formal quotient atlas is a completed etale scheme chart
statement: Let $\Omega$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $\mathcal X$ be a finite-type Deligne--Mumford stack over $\Omega$, and let $x:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\mathcal X$ be a point. Stack, atlas and 2-isomorphism have the meanings in [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]; finite type means that a scheme atlas is locally of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Let $H=\operatorname{Aut}(x)$ be finite, let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a complete Noetherian local $\Omega$-algebra with residue field $\Omega$, and let $f:\operatorname{Spec}R\to\mathcal X$ restrict to $x$ on the closed point. Assume that the formal completion of $\mathcal X$ along the residual gerbe of $x$ is identified with $[\operatorname{Spf}R/H]$, and that the restriction of $f$ is its canonical formal atlas. The residual gerbe is the full substack of objects locally isomorphic to $x$; the quotient classifies $H$-torsors with equivariant maps, and $\operatorname{Spf}R$ is the formal scheme given by the compatible spectra $\operatorname{Spec}(R/\mathfrak m^n)$. Then there exist a finite-type scheme $T$, an etale morphism $a:T\to\mathcal X$, a point $t\in T(\Omega)$ above $x$, an isomorphism of complete local $\Omega$-algebras $R\simeq\widehat{\mathcal O_{T,t}}$, and a 2-isomorphism between $f$ and the composite $\operatorname{Spec}R\simeq\operatorname{Spec}\widehat{\mathcal O_{T,t}}\to T\to\mathcal X$. Completion is maximal-ideal adic [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]; local Noetherian means a unique maximal ideal and the ascending chain condition on ideals [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring].

source.place: Tag 0DQZ (lemma-compare-versal-ring-completion), together with etale.tex Tag 039M (lemma-characterize-etale-completions). Agent-formulated specialization to the given effective formal etale atlas: no existence of a formal quotient presentation is asserted. Pikaart--de Jong, Proposition 2.3.6, printed p.11, uses such an effective atlas; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Apply the complete-pair henselian theorem to $(R,\mathfrak m)$. It is a henselian pair, hence $R$ is a henselian local ring. Its residue field is $\Omega$, which is separably closed: the minimal polynomial of an element of an algebraic field extension has a root in $\Omega$, so its irreducibility forces degree one. Thus $R$ is strictly henselian by the terminology node.

Choose a surjective etale scheme atlas $U\to\mathcal X$ which is locally of finite type over $\Omega$, as allowed by the finite-type hypothesis. The $2$-fibre product $E=\operatorname{Spec}R\times_{\mathcal X}U$ is an algebraic space, etale and surjective over $\operatorname{Spec}R$. Choose a surjective etale scheme cover $W\to E$ from the definition of algebraic space. The calculus applies to these representable maps and makes the composite $W\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ etale and surjective. Use its scheme-chart characterization of surjectivity with the identity chart of the scheme $W$: this scheme map is surjective on points, so there is $y\in W$ above the closed point. The strictly henselian etale-neighbourhood section lemma supplies $\sigma:\operatorname{Spec}R\to W$ over $\operatorname{Spec}R$. The projections of $\sigma$ give an actual morphism $g:\operatorname{Spec}R\to U$ and a $2$-isomorphism $\theta:a g\xrightarrow{\sim}f$.

source.place: Tag 04GG (lemma-characterize-henselian), etale-neighbourhood characterization; the section argument is also read in lean/WeilConjectures/AlgebraicGeometry/Sites/StrictlyHenselian.lean:65-108. Stack base change is as in algebraic.tex Tag 045C.

proof.text: Let $t$ be the $\Omega$-point given by restricting $g$ to the closed point. Its residue field is $\Omega$: the injection $\kappa(t)\to\Omega$ induced by this point has image containing the structural copy of $\Omega$. Choose an affine finite-type neighbourhood $T=\operatorname{Spec}D$ of $t$ in the locally finite-type atlas $U$. Every prime of the local ring $R$ is contained in $\mathfrak m$, so every open subset of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ containing its closed point is all of $\operatorname{Spec}R$. Hence $g$ factors through $T$. The restriction $a:T\to\mathcal X$ is etale by source locality, and $T$ is finite type since its coordinate algebra is finitely generated. Put $A=\mathcal O_{T,t}$ and $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak m_A$. The affine-stalk localization statement identifies $A$ with $D_{\mathfrak p_t}$. The map $D\to R$ of $g$ inverts $D\setminus\mathfrak p_t$, so induces a local $\Omega$-map $u:A\to R$ with identity residue map. The same localization argument applied to $\operatorname{Spec}R$ at its maximal ideal identifies its stalk with $R$. Keep $\theta$ and its closed-point restriction as the chosen framing of $a(t)$ by $x$.

source.place: Affine spectrum and stalk localization; cf. Tag 01HV (lemma-spec-sheaves). The shrinking uses only the displayed prime-ideal argument and the finite-type definition.

proof.text: For any local $\Omega$-algebra $(C,\mathfrak q)$ with residue field $\Omega$ and $\mathfrak q^N=0$, let $\mathcal D_x(C)$ be the groupoid of objects $\xi\in\mathcal X(C)$ with a specified isomorphism $\xi|_\Omega\simeq x$, and arrows respecting that isomorphism. The atlas $a$ identifies this groupoid with the discrete set of maps $b:\operatorname{Spec}C\to T$ reducing to $t$. Indeed, $T\times_{\mathcal X,\xi}\operatorname{Spec}C$ is an etale algebraic space over $\operatorname{Spec}C$; the framing and $t$ specify its section over $\Omega$. Extend this section successively over $C/\mathfrak q^j$, using the unique first order lifting theorem: the kernel $\mathfrak q^j/\mathfrak q^{j+1}$ has square zero for $j\geq1$. Uniqueness makes the final section unique. By the $2$-fibre-product definition, a section is precisely a pair $(b,a(b)\simeq\xi)$ with the specified reduction. For a framed isomorphism $\beta:a(b_1)\simeq a(b_2)$, the pairs $(b_1,\beta)$ and $(b_2,1)$ are sections of $T\times_{\mathcal X,a(b_2)}\operatorname{Spec}C$ with the same closed reduction. Uniqueness gives $b_1=b_2$ and $\beta=1$. This proves full faithfulness as well as essential surjectivity. Uniqueness also makes the identification natural in $C$.

source.place: Tag 0616 (lemma-etale-formally-etale), with definition-formally-smooth-etale-unramified; applied to the etale algebraic-space pullback of the scheme atlas.

proof.text: Use the assumed formal quotient identification to describe the same $\mathcal D_x(C)$. Every such framed object lies in the formal completion: its closed restriction is in the residual gerbe and the ideal $\mathfrak q$ is nilpotent. So it is a pair $(P,v)$ with $P$ an $H$-torsor over $\operatorname{Spec}C$ and $v:P\to\operatorname{Spf}R$ equivariant. The quotient-atlas torsor statement for the trivial action on $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ shows that $P=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is finite etale over $C$. A map from the affine scheme $P$ to $\operatorname{Spf}R$ is a compatible family, that is, an $\Omega$-map $R\to B$ killing some $\mathfrak m^M$. Each automorphism of the local ring $R$ preserves its unique maximal ideal and therefore every $\mathfrak m^M$, so the finite quotients are $H$-stable and $(P,v)$ is a pair for the quotient $[\operatorname{Spec}(R/\mathfrak m^M)/H]$. The quotient-atlas torsor statement identifies its atlas pullback with the finite etale scheme $P\to\operatorname{Spec}C$. The chosen closed framing specifies a section of $P$ over $\Omega$, since $f|_\Omega=x$ and the formal restriction of $f$ is the canonical atlas. Apply the first order lifting theorem along the same powers of $\mathfrak q$ to obtain exactly one section extending it. The section is a pair consisting of a continuous local $\Omega$-map $r:R\to C$ and an isomorphism $q(r)\simeq\xi$; composed with the assumed $2$-isomorphism between the formal restriction of $f$ and $q$, this is an isomorphism $f(r)\simeq\xi$ with the prescribed reduction. For two choices of finite level, pass to a common larger level; the induced torsor sections have the same closed reduction, so unique lifting identifies them. Thus the map $r$ and its framed isomorphism are independent of that choice. As in step 4, uniqueness gives full faithfulness and naturality. Thus $\mathcal D_x(C)$ is also equivalent to the discrete set of these maps $R\to C$.

source.place: Tags 04WM (proposition-equal-quotient-stacks), 0371 (remark-X-mod-G-group), and 0BLZ (lemma-finite-etale-stack), on each nilpotent level; unique lifting is spaces-more-morphisms.tex Tag 0616.

proof.text:
Maps $\operatorname{Spec}C\to T=\operatorname{Spec}D$ reducing to $t$ correspond to local $\Omega$-maps $A=D_{\mathfrak p_t}\to C$: precisely the elements of $D\setminus\mathfrak p_t$ must be inverted, since their residues in $\Omega$ are nonzero. The affine spectrum and localization statements give this correspondence. Combine steps 4 and 5 using the actual isomorphism $\theta:a g\simeq f$. The resulting bijection, for every $C$ under consideration, is exactly
$$\{r:R\to C\text{ local over }\Omega\}\longrightarrow\{h:A\to C\text{ local over }\Omega\},\qquad r\longmapsto r u.$$
This is the displayed map because pulling $\theta$ back by $r$ identifies the atlas lift with $g\circ\operatorname{Spec}r$, whose local ring map is $r u$. Local maps to $C$ are continuous, since they send $\mathfrak m^N$ into $\mathfrak q^N=0$.

source.place: Affine spectrum and stalk localization; explicit calculation of the comparison map, using the two preceding equivalences.

proof.text: For $n\geq1$ put $A_n=A/\mathfrak n^n$ and $R_n=R/\mathfrak m^n$. Both are local $\Omega$-algebras with nilpotent maximal ideal and residue field $\Omega$, so step 6 applies without an Artinian or finite-type requirement on the test. Its surjectivity for $C=A_n$ gives a local map $v_n:R\to A_n$ with $v_n u=q^A_n$. Locality implies $v_n(\mathfrak m^n)=0$, giving $\bar v_n:R_n\to A_n$. Let $u_n:A_n\to R_n$ be induced by $u$. The equation $v_nu=q^A_n$ implies $\bar v_n u_n=1$. The maps $u_n v_n$ and $q^R_n$ from $R$ to $R_n$ become equal after precomposition with $u$, both giving $q^R_n u$. Injectivity in step 6 for $C=R_n$ implies $u_n v_n=q^R_n$, hence $u_n\bar v_n=1$. Therefore every $u_n$ is an isomorphism. For the quotient transitions $p^A_n:A_{n+1}\to A_n$ and $p^R_n:R_{n+1}\to R_n$, the common origin $u$ gives $u_n p^A_n=p^R_n u_{n+1}$. Composing on the left by $\bar v_n$ and on the right by $\bar v_{n+1}$ gives $p^A_n\bar v_{n+1}=\bar v_n p^R_n$, the compatibility needed in step 8.

source.place: Elementary quotient-ring argument from the bijections of step 6. This also identifies the actual maps on completions, rather than an abstract isomorphism of versal rings.

proof.text: By definition $\widehat A=\varprojlim_n A_n$, and completeness identifies $R$ with $\varprojlim_n R_n$. Apply $u_n$ to each coordinate of a compatible sequence to define $\alpha:\widehat A\to R$. Apply $\bar v_n$ to each coordinate for its inverse; step 7 proves the two composites are the identity coordinate by coordinate. Thus $\alpha$ is an isomorphism of complete local $\Omega$-algebras, with $\alpha\circ(A\to\widehat A)=u$. Both maps preserve the adic filtrations: their finite-level reductions are the inverse local maps $u_n,\bar v_n$. Take $R\simeq\widehat A$ to be $\alpha^{-1}$.

source.place: Definition of adic completion as compatible sequences; the inverse-limit argument is written coordinatewise.

proof.text: The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}R\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Spec}\alpha}\operatorname{Spec}\widehat A\to T$ has coordinate ring map $D\to A\to\widehat A\xrightarrow{\alpha}R$, which equals $D\to A\xrightarrow{u}R$ by step 8. This is the coordinate map of $g$, so the two scheme morphisms are equal by the affine spectrum correspondence. Composing with $a$ and then with the already constructed $\theta:a g\simeq f$ supplies the required $2$-isomorphism on all of $\operatorname{Spec}R$. The point $t$, finite-type scheme $T$, etaleness of $a$ and complete-local-ring isomorphism were constructed in steps 2, 3 and 8.

source.place: Affine spectrum correspondence; equality of the two explicit ring maps. The final 2-isomorphism is the actual lift from step 2.
